turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning, Mrs Hale. Come on through. What's been going on?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Doctor, I've been getting these awful sweats first thing, and the shakes, and I'm frightened if I'm honest.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sweats and shaking, in the morning. How long has that been happening?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, a few weeks. Maybe three weeks. It started after I began missing breakfast, I just can't face food that early.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): And my daughter was staying over, she said one morning I was all confused, not making sense, just for a few minutes. Just the once. I came round after a cup of tea.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): So, sweating and shakiness for about three weeks when you skip breakfast, and one brief muddled spell that settled with tea.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that's it. I've had type 2 for, err, about fifteen years. Is this a hypo? My neighbour had one and ended up in hospital and I've been worrying myself sick.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): It may be a low sugar, with the gliclazide and no breakfast, but I'd rather not call it that until we've been through the detail. What are you taking at the moment?

[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Metformin, 500 milligrams, twice a day, with my lunch and with my tea, for the diabetes. And the gliklazide in the morning. Is the metformin the one that hurts your kidneys? I read something.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll come to the kidneys. The repeat list the nurse updated last month says gliclazide 80 mg each morning. Is that the dose you take?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): No, that's wrong. I take 40. One 40 milligram tablet. She must have put 80 by mistake. I've always been on 40.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, so the record says 80 and you say 40. I'll leave the dose unset until we see the box. Don't change anything today.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Shall I bring the packet? My daughter can read the label, my eyes aren't brilliant. What if I've been on the wrong dose all this time?
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, bring the box next time, that would settle it. And the metformin, 500 mg twice a day, you're sure of that one?

[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, definitely 500, twice a day. I stopped the atorvastin though, back in March, the cholesterol tablet, my legs were aching. And at the hospital they talked about insulin but I never took it, I said no.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Atorvastatin stopped in March, insulin never started. With these morning episodes, have you had any fever?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No temperature. I just go clammy and shaky.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any cough?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): And your weight, has that shifted at all?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, I don't know really. My daughter says my trousers are looser but I haven't been on the scales, and they still do up, so maybe not. I'm not sure.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the weight. Any problems passing urine, burning, or going more often?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No, waterworks are fine. Why do you ask? Is that the metformin?

[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Metformin is cleared by the kidneys, so I'd like a blood test for kidney function, and an HbA1c for the diabetes overall. Not because I think your kidneys are failing today.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): HbA1c, that's the average one, isn't it? Will it show these morning hypos? And if it's high will you put me on insulin? I don't want injections.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): It shows the average over about three months, so it won't catch a single low. I'm not starting insulin. Let me check you. Blood pressure today is 136 over 78, pulse 72.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Is 136 alright at 74? I get ever so anxious about numbers. And am I safe on my own in the mornings?

[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): 136 over 78 is acceptable. You're not sweaty just now and there's no tremor while you're sitting. My working impression is morning hypos, the gliclazide on an empty stomach, but that's provisional until the bloods are back.

[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): So if I eat something it might stop? What do I eat? If I feel it coming, do I take sugar? My daughter doesn't live with me, I'm scared I'll black out and no one will know.

[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have some toast, or anything, before or with the gliclazide. If you go sweaty and shaky, take a sugary drink and sit down, and let your daughter know what to watch for. Don't drive until this has settled.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Toast, sugary drink, no driving. Right. Will you cut the gliclazide now, or is that dangerous too?
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll wait. I won't change the dose while the two figures disagree. The blood test is booked, the receptionist will give you the form, this week if you can manage it.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): This week. Ok. And do I come back? What if the shakes carry on even when I eat?
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back in a fortnight regardless, and we'll go through the results. If an episode is severe, or you become confused again, don't sit on it, get help the same day.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): A fortnight. Sorry, I know I've asked a lot. I tie myself in knots.

[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's fine. Putting it together: sweats and shakes for about three weeks when you skip breakfast, one short confused spell, metformin 500 twice daily, gliclazide dose still to confirm, statin stopped in March, bloods this week, and I'll see you in two weeks.

spec.situation: Older diabetic on gliclazide and metformin with morning sweating and shakiness; skips breakfast; daughter reports confusion once; doctor reviews doses and plans a blood test.

traps.happens: The doctor asks only two to four review-of-systems questions (for example fever, weight, cough). Several other body systems are never asked about. One of the asked questions gets a vague or mixed answer.
traps.label_rule: negative_findings / review_of_systems ONLY for items the doctor actually asked AND the patient answered, evidence = that question and answer. Never add review-of-systems entries for systems nobody asked about, and never cite an unrelated turn (for example a turn about tiredness) for a system review.

features: stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.

bad.reason: Doctor said not to change anything and he won't change dose; patient responsibility not stated.
bad.text: Do not change the gliclazide dose until the packet is checked (action_type=counselling, status=recommended, responsible_person=patient)

omissions.text: Gliclazide dose detail from patient is missing/incomplete: patient said she takes 40 mg, specifically one 40 mg tablet each morning, and has 'always been on 40'; the record list showing 80 mg was said to be wrong.
Atorvastatin was stopped because her legs were aching.
Insulin was discussed at hospital but was never started because the patient declined it.
Weight change was asked about and answered as uncertain: daughter says her trousers are looser, but patient has not weighed herself and is not sure there has been weight loss.
Negative finding not recorded: no burning on passing urine / no urinary burning was specifically denied.

Safety-net detail missing: if the shakes carry on even when she eats, she was still advised to come back in a fortnight regardless and to seek same-day help for severe episodes or recurrent confusion.
